01.r: A narrative opening that sets the scene.
01.n: Literally 'it became' or 'it happened', followed directly by the next verb with no 'that' in the Greek; English needs the 'that'. Five of the six translations keep the traditional 'it came to pass'.

02.r: Moves the story on to a new section.

04.r: The article with 'days'; English uses 'those' alone.

05.r: The period of the events just told.

06.r: Points back to the time of the events before.

08.r: A public order from the emperor.
08.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'a public decree, ordinance', and lists this verse under the decrees of Roman rulers.

09.r: Caesar is the source of the decree.

11.r: The emperor who ruled at the time of Jesus' birth.
11.n: Abbott-Smith marks the name as Latin and lists this verse as its only New Testament use. He refers the reader to Σεβαστός for comparison.

12.r: To have one's name entered on an official list.
12.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to enrol', and for the middle 'to enrol oneself', citing this verse, though he points to a commentary that reads it otherwise; the form can be middle or passive. The word is about writing names on a register, not about paying. The KJV and Geneva's 'taxed' likely reflects the purpose of such a registration, which was taxation, but that is an inference the word itself does not carry.

13.r: The whole of the world in question.

15.n: Literally 'the inhabited (earth)', a participle of the verb 'to dwell'. Abbott-Smith records that in later writers it came to mean the Roman world, which is the BSB's 'empire'.
